what_its_for: Fosaprepitant is used to help prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy (cancer treatment). It is usually given along with other anti-nausea medicines to give you the best protection against feeling sick during and after your cancer treatment.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. You will receive this infusion at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. You do not take this medicine at home by mouth. The infusion usually takes about 20 to 30 minutes. Make sure to tell your nurse or doctor if you feel any pain, burning, or swelling at the injection site during the infusion.
dosing: The typical dose is 150 mg given as a single IV infusion on the first day of your chemotherapy cycle, about 30 minutes before your chemotherapy begins. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on your specific chemotherapy regimen and your overall health. Always follow the exact dosing schedule your doctor or care team gives you.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare professional at your scheduled appointment, a missed dose is unlikely. However, if you miss or have to reschedule your chemotherapy appointment, contact your doctor or care team right away so they can reschedule your infusion and make sure your anti-nausea treatment plan stays on track.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. If for any reason you are given information about storage, keep it at room temperature away from light and heat, and never freeze it. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medications you take, including vitamins, supplements, and herbal products, because fosaprepitant can interact with many medicines. Avoid taking warfarin (a blood thinner) without close monitoring, as this medicine may lower its effectiveness. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not start or stop any medications without talking to your doctor first. Avoid alcohol during your chemotherapy period as it can worsen nausea.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, itching, swelling of face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, or dizziness); severe skin reactions such as blistering or peeling skin; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of a blood clot (pain, redness, or swelling in your arm or leg); or any new or worsening symptoms after your infusion. Also call your doctor if your nausea or vomiting is not well controlled.
when_it_works: Fosaprepitant starts working quickly after it is infused into your vein. It works by blocking a substance in your body called substance P that triggers nausea and vomiting. It is most effective when given together with other anti-nausea medicines as directed by your doctor. The protection it provides can last for several days after your chemotherapy treatment.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This medicine may affect how well hormonal birth control (like pills, patches, or implants) works for up to 28 days after your dose, so use a backup method of birth control during this time. Elderly patients: Older adults can generally use this medicine safely, but should be monitored closely. Liver disease: If you have severe liver problems, tell your doctor, as dose adjustments may be needed. Children: This medicine may be used in children in certain situations; your child's doctor will determine the appropriate dose.
